titel: Ars brevis (1308) — prologue, alphabet and figures
quelle: Ars brevis (Pisa, 1308). Latin text after the Strasbourg edition of 1617 (Zetzner: Raymundi Lullii Opera ea quae ad adinventam ab ipso artem universalem pertinent), from the Internet Archive scan of the Bibliothèque interuniversitaire de Santé copy, OCR emended by hand against the standard textual tradition. Public domain; the modern critical edition (ROL) remains in copyright and is not used.
hinweis: A prologue module, not an edition of the whole work: the invocation, the prologue, the alphabet, the first figure, and the fourth figure — the three rotating paper wheels that generate 252 combinatorial chambers, the device Leibniz named as the inspiration of his ars combinatoria. The English is an unofficial working translation made for this site — cite the Latin. The figures themselves are not reproduced; the paragraph numbers are editorial.

units.label: Invocatio
units.orig: Deus, cum tua gratia, sapientia et amore, incipit Ars brevis, quae est imago Artis generalis, quae sic intitulatur: Deus, cum tua summa perfectione, incipit Ars generalis ultima.
units.txt: God, with thy grace, wisdom and love, here begins the Brief Art, which is an image of the General Art, which is entitled thus: God, with thy highest perfection, here begins the last General Art.

units.label: Prologus
units.orig: Ratio quare facimus istam Artem brevem est, ut Ars magna facilius sciatur. Nam, scita ista Arte, et supradicta et etiam aliae artes de facili possunt sciri et addisci. Subiectum huius Artis est respondere de omnibus quaestionibus, supposito quod sciatur quid dicitur per nomen. Et dividitur iste liber in tredecim partes, in quas similiter Ars magna est divisa. Prima pars est de alphabeto. Secunda de figuris. Tertia de definitionibus. Quarta de regulis. Quinta de tabula. Sexta de evacuatione tertiae figurae. Septima de multiplicatione quartae figurae. Octava de mixtione principiorum et regularum. Nona de novem subiectis. Decima de applicatione. Undecima de quaestionibus. Duodecima de habituatione. Tertiadecima de modo docendi hanc Artem. Et primo de prima dicimus sic.
units.txt: The reason why we make this Brief Art is that the Great Art may be known more easily. For once this Art is known, the one named above, and other arts too, can easily be known and learnt. The subject of this Art is to answer all questions, provided that what is meant by a name be known. And this book is divided into thirteen parts, into which the Great Art is likewise divided. The first part is on the alphabet; the second on the figures; the third on the definitions; the fourth on the rules; the fifth on the table; the sixth on the emptying of the third figure; the seventh on the multiplication of the fourth figure; the eighth on the mixture of principles and rules; the ninth on the nine subjects; the tenth on application; the eleventh on questions; the twelfth on habituation; the thirteenth on the manner of teaching this Art. And first, of the first part, we speak as follows.

units.label: Pars I — De alphabeto
units.orig: Alphabetum ponimus in hac Arte, ut per ipsum possimus facere figuras, et etiam miscere principia et regulas ad investigandam veritatem. Nam per unam literam habentem multa significata intellectus est magis generalis ad respiciendum multa significata, et etiam ad faciendam scientiam. Et ipsum quidem alphabetum oportet corde tenus scire; aliter enim artista Arte ista non poterit bene uti.
units.txt: We set an alphabet into this Art, so that by it we may make the figures, and also mix the principles and rules in order to investigate the truth. For through one letter that has many meanings the intellect becomes more general in surveying many meanings, and also in making science. And this alphabet must be known by heart; for otherwise the artist will not be able to use this Art well.

units.label: The alphabet B–K
units.orig: B significat bonitatem, differentiam, utrum, Deum, iustitiam, avaritiam. C significat magnitudinem, concordantiam, quid, angelum, prudentiam, gulam. D significat durationem, contrarietatem, de quo, caelum, fortitudinem, luxuriam. E significat potestatem, principium, quare, hominem, temperantiam, superbiam. F significat sapientiam, medium, quantum, imaginativam, fidem, accidiam. G significat voluntatem, finem, quale, sensitivam, spem, invidiam. H significat virtutem, maioritatem, quando, vegetativam, caritatem, iram. I significat veritatem, aequalitatem, ubi, elementativam, patientiam, mendacium. K significat gloriam, minoritatem, quomodo et cum quo, instrumentativam, pietatem, inconstantiam.
units.txt: B signifies goodness, difference, whether, God, justice, avarice. C signifies greatness, concordance, what, angel, prudence, gluttony. D signifies duration, contrariety, of what, heaven, fortitude, lust. E signifies power, beginning, why, man, temperance, pride. F signifies wisdom, middle, how much, the imaginative faculty, faith, sloth. G signifies will, end, of what quality, the sensitive faculty, hope, envy. H signifies virtue, majority, when, the vegetative faculty, charity, wrath. I signifies truth, equality, where, the elementative faculty, patience, lying. K signifies glory, minority, how and with what, the instrumentative faculty, piety, inconstancy.

units.label: Pars II — De prima figura
units.orig: Pars ista in quatuor partes dividitur, videlicet in quatuor figuras. Prima figura est de A. Ipsa quidem figura continet in se novem principia, videlicet bonitatem, magnitudinem etc., et novem literas, videlicet b, c, d, e etc. Ipsa quidem figura est circularis, eo quod subiectum mutatur in praedicatum, et e converso, ut cum dicitur: bonitas est magna, et magnitudo est bona, et sic de aliis. In ipsa quidem figura inquirit artista naturalem coniunctionem inter subiectum et praedicatum, dispositionem et proportionem, ut ad faciendum conclusionem possit medium invenire. Quodlibet enim principium per se sumptum est omnino generale, ut cum dicitur bonitas et magnitudo. Quando autem unum principium contrahitur ad aliud, tunc ipsum est subalternatum, ut cum dicitur bonitas magna. Et quando contrahitur aliquod principium ad singulare, tunc est principium specialissimum, ut cum dicitur: bonitas Petri est magna. Et sic intellectus habet scalam ascendendi et descendendi a principio omnino generali ad non omnino generale, et ad omnino speciale. Et sic de ascensu et descensu istius scalae potest dici suo modo.
units.txt: This part is divided into four parts, namely into four figures. The first figure is that of A. This figure contains in itself nine principles — namely goodness, greatness and so on — and nine letters, namely b, c, d, e and so on. And this figure is circular, because the subject is changed into the predicate and conversely, as when one says: goodness is great, and greatness is good, and so with the others. In this figure the artist seeks the natural conjunction between subject and predicate, their disposition and proportion, so that he may find the middle term for making a conclusion. For every principle taken by itself is wholly general, as when goodness or greatness is spoken of. But when one principle is contracted to another, it is subalternate, as when one says great goodness. And when some principle is contracted to a singular, it is a most special principle, as when one says: the goodness of Peter is great. And thus the intellect has a ladder for ascending and descending, from the wholly general principle to one not wholly general, and to the wholly special. And of the ascent and descent of this ladder more can be said in its own manner.

units.label: De prima figura (conclusion)
units.orig: In principiis istius figurae est implicatum quicquid est. Nam quicquid est, aut est bonum aut magnum etc., sicut Deus et angelus, qui sunt boni et magni etc. Quapropter quicquid est, reducibile est ad principia supradicta.
units.txt: In the principles of this figure everything that exists is implicated. For whatever exists is either good or great, and so on — as God and angel, who are good and great, and so forth. Wherefore whatever exists is reducible to the principles named above.

units.label: Pars II, cap. V — De quarta figura (the rotating wheels)
units.orig: Quarta figura habet tres circulos, quorum superior est immobilis, duo autem inferiores sunt mobiles, ut in figura patet. Circulus medius volvitur sub circulo superiori immobili, ut puta quando ponitur c sub b; circulus autem inferior volvitur sub circulo medio, sicut quando ponitur d sub c. Et tunc temporis formantur novem camerae: b c d est una camera, c d e est alia, et sic de aliis deinceps. E circuli minoris ponatur sub c circuli mediocris, et tunc temporis formantur aliae novem camerae: b c e est una camera, et c d f alia. Et cum omnes literae circuli minoris erunt discursae cum b circuli maioris et cum c circuli mediocris, tunc temporis c est medium inter b et d, eo quia b et d participant inter se ad invicem per significata de c; et sic de aliis cameris. Sic per media camerarum homo venatur necessarias conclusiones et invenit illas. Iterum discurrantur literae cum b eiusdem circuli maioris et cum d circuli mediocris, et sic de aliis circuli mediocris et circuli inferioris, mutando illas, b circuli maioris existente immobili, usque quo perveniatur cum b circuli maioris ad i circuli mediocris et ad k circuli inferioris; et sic erunt ducentae quinquaginta et duae camerae. [figure omitted]
units.txt: The fourth figure has three circles, of which the uppermost is immobile, while the two lower ones are mobile, as appears in the figure. The middle circle turns beneath the immobile upper circle — as, say, when c is placed under b; and the lower circle turns beneath the middle one, as when d is placed under c. And then nine chambers are formed: b c d is one chamber, c d e is another, and so on with the rest. Let e of the smallest circle be placed under c of the middle circle, and then another nine chambers are formed: b c e is one chamber, and c d f another. And when all the letters of the smallest circle have been run through against b of the greatest circle and c of the middle circle, then c is the middle term between b and d, because b and d participate in one another through the meanings of c; and so with the other chambers. Thus by the middle terms of the chambers a man hunts down necessary conclusions and finds them. Again, let the letters be run through with b of the same greatest circle and d of the middle circle, and so on with the others of the middle and the lower circle, changing them while b of the greatest circle stands immobile, until with b of the greatest circle one arrives at i of the middle circle and k of the lowest; and thus there will be two hundred and fifty-two chambers. [figure omitted]

units.label: De quarta figura (conclusion)
units.orig: Figura ista generalior est quam tertia, quia in qualibet camera istius quartae figurae sunt tres literae, sed in qualibet camera tertiae figurae non sunt nisi duae literae; ideo intellectus generalior est per quartam figuram quam per tertiam.
units.txt: This figure is more general than the third, because in each chamber of this fourth figure there are three letters, while in each chamber of the third figure there are only two; therefore the intellect is more general through the fourth figure than through the third.
